cards.title: Nothing arrives unless you ask
cards.body:
Every web page, picture and video you've ever seen online arrived because your [[browser]] **asked** for it. Websites never just push pages at you.

The asking and answering follows a [[protocol]] you met in the last module: **HTTP**. Let's see what those messages actually look like.

cards.title: Requests
cards.body:
**HTTP** stands for **HyperText Transfer [[Protocol]]** (*hypertext* just means text with links). Your [[browser]] (the **client**) sends a **request**, and the [[server]] sends back a **response**. A simple request looks like this:

`GET /news HTTP/1.1`
`Host: example.com`

The first line says what to do (`GET`, a **method**), which page (`/news`, the **path**), and the HTTP version. The `Host` line is a **header** that says which website you mean, because one server can host many sites.

cards.title: Responses
cards.body: The [[server]]'s **response** starts with a **status line**, like `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, that says how it went. More [[headers|header]] follow, then the **body**: the page's content itself, usually written in **HTML** (the code that describes a web page).

cards.prompt: Match each part of an [[HTTP]] message to its job.

pairs.right: What you want the server to do
Which page or file you want
Which website on the server you mean
The content itself, like the page's HTML

cards.explanation: The **method** is the action, the **path** is which item, and the **Host** header picks the website. The response **body** carries the actual content, like the HTML that describes the page.
cards.hint: Think of ordering from a shop: one part is the action, one is which item, one is which shop, and one is what you get back.
cards.nudge: Look back at `GET /news` and the `Host` line: the first word is the action, the next is which page. The body only comes back in the response.

cards.title: GET and POST
cards.body:
The two methods you'll meet most are:

- **GET**: "please give me this". It's used for loading pages, pictures and videos. Almost everything you do while browsing is a GET.
- **POST**: "please take this data". It's used for sending something to the [[server]], like filling in a form, logging in, posting a comment or uploading a photo. The data travels in the request's body.

There are a few other methods too, but GET and POST do most of the work on the web. Each file (the page itself, and every picture on it) is fetched with its own GET request.

cards.prompt: You fill in a sign-up form and press **Create account**. Which method does the [[browser]] most likely use?

options.nudge: GET is for fetching pages and pictures. When you press Create account, which way is your data travelling?
SYN is part of TCP's handshake, not an HTTP method. Pick one of the two methods from the lesson.
MX is a kind of DNS record, not an HTTP method. Which method is for sending data to a server?

cards.explanation: You're **sending** data (your name, email and password) to the server, so it's a **POST**. GET is for fetching things. SYN is part of TCP's [[handshake]], and MX is a [[DNS]] record type: neither is an [[HTTP]] method.
cards.hint: Are you fetching something here, or sending your details to the [[server]]?

cards.title: Status codes
cards.body:
Every response has a three-digit **status code**. The **first digit** tells you the kind of answer:

- **2xx**: success
- **3xx**: redirect (look somewhere else)
- **4xx**: a problem with the request, like asking for something that isn't there
- **5xx**: a problem on the [[server]]

Four you'll see often: **200 OK** (here it is), **301 Moved Permanently** (it's at a new address now, go there), **404 Not Found** (there's nothing at that path) and **500 Internal Server Error** (something broke on the server).

cards.prompt: Match each [[status code]] to its meaning.

pairs.right: OK: here's what you asked for
Moved permanently to a new address
Not found: nothing at that path
Something went wrong on the server

cards.explanation: **200** is success, **301** is a permanent redirect, **404** means the path doesn't exist, and **500** means the server hit an error. Check the first digit: 2 success, 3 redirect, 4 request problem, 5 server problem.
cards.hint: Use the first digit: 2 is success, 3 is a redirect, 4 is a problem with the request, and 5 is a problem on the server.
cards.nudge: Check the first digit of each code again. A 4 means the request asked for something wrong, while a 5 means the server itself broke.

cards.prompt: `curl -I` (that's a capital **I**, for *information*) asks a [[server]] for just the [[headers|header]] of a response, without the page itself. Run it on `http://example.com/old-news` and find where that page has moved to. (The other two pages are there to compare, if you're curious.)
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Get the response headers for the home page
commands.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 1256
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 10:20:15 GMT
Server: nginx

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: http://example.com/news
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 169
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 10:20:21 GMT
Server: nginx

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 153
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 10:20:27 GMT
Server: nginx

cards.explanation:
`/old-news` answered **301 Moved Permanently**, and its `Location` header says the new address: `http://example.com/news`. A [[browser]] would follow that automatically. The home page gave **200 OK**, and `/missing` gave **404 Not Found**.

(`curl -I` actually sends a **HEAD** request, which is like GET but asks for the headers only.)
cards.hint: Run `curl -I http://example.com/old-news`. A redirect has a header that gives the new address: look for the line labelled `Location`.
cards.nudge: Make sure you ran it on `/old-news`, not the other pages. The status line says it moved; the new address is on the `Location` line.

cards.prompt: A web page is made of 1 [[HTML]] file, 3 images and 1 stylesheet (a file describing colours and layout). The [[browser]] has none of them saved yet. At least how many [[HTTP]] requests does it make to load the page?
cards.explanation: Each file is fetched with its own request: 1 + 3 + 1 = **5**. First the browser GETs the HTML, reads it, discovers it needs 3 images and a stylesheet, and requests those too. Big websites can need over a hundred requests for a single page.
cards.hint: Each file is fetched with its own request. Count every file the page needs, including the HTML itself.
cards.nudge: Don't forget the HTML file: the browser has to fetch it first before it knows about the images and the stylesheet.

cards.prompt: A page shows **500 Internal Server Error**. What does that tell you?

options.text: Something went wrong on the server, but your connection works: a response arrived

options.nudge: If your Wi-Fi were down, no response would arrive at all. Here a status code came back, so your connection worked.
A page that doesn't exist gives a 4xx code, like 404. What does a code starting with 5 mean?
A wrong address would give a 4xx code, a problem with the request. Codes starting with 5 point somewhere else.

cards.explanation: A **5xx** code means the **server** had a problem. And the fact that you got any response at all proves your connection, [[DNS]] and the route to the server all worked. A page that doesn't exist or a typo in the path would give a **4xx** code, like 404, instead.
cards.hint: Look at the first digit of the code. Which kind of problem does a 5 point to? And notice that a response arrived at all.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **HTTP** is request and response: the [[browser]] asks, the [[server]] answers.
- A request has a **method**, a **path** and **headers** like `Host`. A response has a **status code**, headers and a **body**.
- **GET** fetches things, and **POST** sends data.
- Status codes: **2xx** success, **3xx** redirect, **4xx** request problem, **5xx** server problem. Know 200, 301, 404 and 500.

Next: keeping all of this private with [[HTTPS]].
